Before you begin

The Newspaper That Drew the Argument

For half a century, Harper's Weekly (1857–1916) was the most widely read newspaper in the United States. It called itself "A Journal of Civilization," and in an age before photographs could be printed, its full-page wood engravings carried the news as pictures — battles, portraits, and, above all, political cartoons.

Its most powerful artist was Thomas Nast. His drawings helped elect presidents, defended emancipation and Black citizenship, and attacked the terror that undid Reconstruction. A single Nast engraving could shape how millions of Americans felt about an issue — which is exactly what made the magazine so powerful, and so worth reading carefully.

Every image here was built to persuade. As you look, ask: who is the hero, who is the villain, and what does the artist want you to believe?

The War & Emancipation · 1864–1865

“Compromise with the South” (1864)

Nast's warning in the 1864 election year: to make peace with the Confederacy now would betray every Union soldier who had died. A triumphant Confederate shakes hands over a Union grave.

“Compromise with the South” — wood engraving by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, 1864, public domain (Library of Congress)

The War & Emancipation · 1864–1865

“Franchise — And Not This Man?” (1865)

Columbia points to a wounded Black veteran and asks the nation whether he, who fought for the Union, should be denied the vote. An argument for Black suffrage at the war's end.

“Franchise — And Not This Man?” — wood engraving by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, 1865, public domain (Library of Congress)

The War & Emancipation · 1864–1865

“Emancipation” (1865)

Nast's sweeping vision of freedom: the horrors of slavery on the left, a hopeful future of family, school, and paid work on the right, with Lincoln below.

“Emancipation” — wood engraving by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, 1865, public domain (Library of Congress)

Reconstruction & Its Undoing · 1866–1874

“Slavery Is Dead?” (1867)

Two panels ask whether slavery truly ended: a Black man sold for a crime in 'the Land of the Free,' and whipped as punishment in 'the Home of the Brave.' Nast's challenge to the Black Codes.

“(?) Slavery Is Dead (?)” — wood engraving by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, 1867, public domain (Library of Congress)

Reconstruction & Its Undoing · 1866–1874

“The First Vote” (1867)

The magazine's most famous Reconstruction cover: Black men — a craftsman, a city man, a soldier — line up to cast their first ballots. Drawn by A. R. Waud.

“The First Vote” — wood engraving by Alfred R. Waud, Harper's Weekly, 1867, public domain (Library of Congress)

Reconstruction & Its Undoing · 1866–1874

The Senate as a Court of Impeachment (1868)

The packed Senate chamber during the impeachment trial of President Andrew Johnson — the first time a president faced removal.

The Senate as a Court of Impeachment — wood engraving, Harper's Weekly, 1868, public domain (Library of Congress)

Reconstruction & Its Undoing · 1866–1874

“This Is a White Man's Government” (1868)

Three enemies of Reconstruction — an Irish immigrant, a Confederate, and a Northern financier — stand on a fallen Black veteran. One of Nast's sharpest attacks.

“This Is a White Man's Government” — wood engraving by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, 1868, public domain (Library of Congress)

Reconstruction & Its Undoing · 1866–1874

“Worse Than Slavery” (1874)

A hooded Klansman and a White League member join hands over a terrorized Black family, beneath a skull reading 'Worse Than Slavery.' Nast's indictment of Reconstruction violence.

“Worse Than Slavery” — wood engraving by Thomas Nast, Harper's Weekly, 1874, public domain (Library of Congress)

Reading like a historian

Pictures Are Arguments

A cartoon is a primary source with a point of view. When you analyze one, name what you see (people, symbols, words), decide what the artist is claiming, and judge whether the claim is fair. That is the same skill the ACT rewards when it asks you to find an author's purpose and argument.

Want higher-resolution copies for your own projects? Many Harper's Weekly engravings are free to download from the Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access collection (CC0) and the Library of Congress.
